source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning (Table 1, aggregation strategies)
finding: Weighting sampled paths by raw sequence probability (a code-length rule) does far worse than majority vote. Only length-normalised weighting matches majority vote.
numbers: PaLM-540B, GSM8K: greedy 56.5, weighted avg unnormalised 56.3, weighted sum unnormalised 59.9, weighted sum normalised 74.1, majority vote 74.4. AQuA: 35.8 / 35.8 / 38.2 / 48.0 / 48.3. MultiArith: 94.7 / 90.5 / 92.2 / 99.3 / 99.3.
limits: 2022 PaLM-540B only. Argmax of raw probability alone is not tested; the unnormalised weighted average is the closest. Read via ar5iv.
agent_relevance: Old direct evidence for gap 1: pure raw-code-length selection loses about 18 points to voting on GSM8K. Use likelihood as a weight inside a vote or as a tie-break.

source: Kang, Zhao, Song (2025) Scalable Best-of-N Selection via Self-Certainty (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Self-certainty (mean KL from uniform of the token distribution) and perplexity both trail plain self-consistency on definitive-answer math at the same N. Perplexity correlates with length and favours no-answer responses.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 4-dataset average: self-consistency 56.15, self-certainty 52.71, perplexity 51.08, Borda vote 56.51. MATH N=64: SC 63.40, certainty 56.70, perplexity 51.96. GSM8K N=64: 90.99 vs 88.90. R1-Distill-Llama-8B MATH L3 N=64: SC 87.62, certainty 84.08, Borda 88.06.
limits: Mostly one 8B model; several tables single-trial. All methods use the same samples, so equal tokens. Confidence can be distorted by overconfident samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 largely answered: likelihood-type scores alone do not beat voting at equal samples; combining them (Borda) gives +0.3 to +0.7. A pure description-length score has a length bias.

source: Leang et al. (2025) PiCSAR: Probabilistic Confidence Selection And Ranking
finding: PiCSAR picks the sample with the highest joint log-probability of reasoning chain plus answer, log p(r|x)+log p(y|a,r,x). This is a code-length (MAP) rule. It beats self-consistency, USC and self-certainty in 37 of 40 comparisons.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B GPQA-D: self-certainty 26.54 to PiCSAR 29.80 (+3.26). Llama-3.1-70B: +7.07 over self-certainty, +5.66 over USC. Qwen3-8B: 41.25 (SC) to 46.98. Reasoning models, k=6: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B +12.33 (AIME24) and +12.78 (AIME25) over SC. PiCSAR at k=6 beats 16 of 20 baselines run at k=16 or 32. Information plane (Llama-3.1-8B, MATH500, k=6): high-high quadrant 71.7% accuracy; other quadrants 39.0, 31.6, 62.2.
limits: Needs an extra forward pass and answer prompt for the answer term. Gains shrink or vanish for Qwen3 non-thinking models on easy sets. Single preprint. Table text was garbled in extraction; headline numbers are from the paper text.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 1: summed-log-prob selection can beat voting at equal or fewer samples, with and without length normalisation (PiCSAR-N). No explicit prior term was tested. Cheap to copy when logprobs are exposed.

source: Leang et al. (2025) PiCSAR, Table 4 (rank by score vs length and accuracy)
finding: Chains ranked lowest by the joint score are much longer and less accurate. Shorter, information-dense chains are more often right.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B: highest-score group 16.43 sentences and 53.33% accuracy; lowest group 64.72 sentences and 44.20%. In every one of the 5 model blocks the highest-score group is the most accurate (last block 46.53 vs 41.60).
limits: Correlational. Peak-to-sentence ratio is a defined proxy (95th percentile of correct-sample confidence).
agent_relevance: Supports gap 4: log-prob and token count of a chain track correctness; shorter and higher-probability is better within a question.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains
finding: Within one question, the shortest sampled reasoning chain is most often correct. short-m@k (stop after the first m chains finish, then vote) matches or beats majority voting with fewer tokens.
numbers: 4 reasoning models (LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B), AIME24/25, HMMT, GPQA-D, 20 samples each. LN-Super-49B math avg: random 47.7, longest 28.9, shortest 63.4. R1-670B math: 78.2 / 58.9 / 83.3. short-1@k uses up to 40% fewer thinking tokens than majority; short-3@k up to 33% less wall time, about +2% (QwQ) and +4% (R1-670B) at 80k-100k tokens. Finetune on shortest chains: 57.9% vs random 56.3%.
limits: 30 problems per math set. On GPQA-D R1-670B shortest (75.8) is slightly below random (76.2). Reasoning models only; a within-question effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered yes for reasoning models at equal or lower tokens. Cheap rule: prefer the shortest finished chain, then vote. This is MDL's Occam preference as token count.

source: Authors not read (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? (arXiv 2506.04210)
finding: Accuracy rises then falls with thinking length. Longer thinking raises output variance (entropy). Parallel sampling with voting beats extended sequential thinking.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: 82.2% at about 385 tokens, 87.3% at about 1,100 (peak), 70.3% at about 15,980. MATH-500: baseline 83.2%, falls to 78.3% at about 16k tokens. Entropy 0.23 to 2.79 on GSM8K. Parallel thinking up to 22% better than Wait-and-Think-More at 16K tokens.
limits: Small distilled models (1.5B, 7B, 8B); GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24. Source text has rendering typos.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 4: past a point, more reasoning tokens add description length without evidence. Argues for several short chains plus a selector over one long chain.

source: Authors not read (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Weighted Voting (arXiv 2511.02309)
finding: At matched token budget, sequential refinement chains beat parallel self-consistency, and entropy-weighted voting beats plain majority.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Qwen3-30B/235B, Kimi-K2), AIME24, AIME25, GPQA-D, 3/6/9 chains of 4,096 tokens. Sequential wins 43 of 45 configs; max gap Qwen3-235B AIME25 6 chains 76.7% vs 30.0%. Inverse-entropy weighting best in 29 of 30 sequential configs. Parallel entropy-weighted beats majority in 6 of 6 configs, by +0.5 to +3.4 points.
limits: 30 problems per set, so 1-2 problems flip results. Math and science only. Sequential costs latency. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial: a confidence weight (low entropy, short code) inside the vote helps at equal tokens, but parallel gains are small.

source: Authors not read (2025) Think Deep, Think Fast: verifier-free inference-time scaling (arXiv 2504.14047)
finding: For reasoning models, plain majority voting beats best-of-N, sequential revision and mixture-of-agents. Shorter responses are more often correct for reasoning models; non-reasoning models show no stable length effect.
numbers: 11 models, MATH-500, AIME24 (30 problems), GPQA-D; 100 samples for reasoning models, 256 for non-reasoning. Logistic regression on marker counts: test F1 0.7469 (R1-Distill-Llama-70B) and 0.8637 (R1-Distill-Llama-14B).
limits: Best-of-N here uses an LLM judge, not log-probability, so it does not test a likelihood rule. No token budgets. Exact gaps only in figures.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: voting is a hard baseline that any code-length selector must beat. The length effect holds for reasoning models only, so gate it by model type.

source: Authors not read (2026) Model Capability Dominates: Inference-Time Optimization Lessons from AIMO 3 (arXiv 2603.27844)
finding: In a math olympiad competition, model choice mattered far more than selection tricks. Entropy-weighted voting tied plain voting locally.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b N=8: 39.3 mean over 21 runs (range 34-42) vs gpt-oss-20b 31.0. gpt-oss-20b at N=32 fell to 26 (per-attempt accuracy 0.61 to 0.52) because time per attempt shrank. Entropy-weighted vote (Qwen3.5-35B, N=16): 8/10, equal to baseline. Pass@20 about 45.5.
limits: Local tests are small (10 problems). No verifier tested. Prompt changes moved scores by about +/-2.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the gap between pass@k and majority (about 6 points here) is the ceiling any selector could gain; likelihood weighting added nothing locally.

source: Bhide, Gupta, Cunningham, Domke (2026) Stacking-Based Weighting for Large Language Bayes in M-Open Settings
finding: When an LLM writes many candidate probabilistic programs, marginal-likelihood weighting (Bayesian model averaging) puts almost all weight on one model under misspecification. Stacking on predictive score spreads the weight and matches held-out score.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B wrote 250 NumPyro programs per task; 3 FEMA loss tasks (20 train, 10 test counties). BMA weight on top model: 1.000 (hurricane, inland flood), 0.998 (wildfire). Held-out ELPD BMA vs stacking: -5.983 vs -5.999; -370.340 vs -370.340; -177.922 vs -177.897. Stacking weights e.g. 0.759, 0.238, 0.003.
limits: Three tasks; stacking gives no accuracy gain, only more dispersed weights. Number of surviving programs not stated. ELBO is only a bound on leave-one-out.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 7 partial: marginal likelihood concentrates on one candidate under misspecification, and a hold-out predictive weight is a safe equal-quality alternative. This is the SafeBayes concern, but no tempering was tested.

source: Authors not read (2026) RIMRULE: Improving Tool-Using Language Agents via MDL-Guided Rule Learning (ACL 2026)
finding: An LLM agent distils rules from failure traces, and an MDL objective (rule symbol length plus failures left uncorrected) consolidates them. MDL consolidation beats prompt-based consolidation.
numbers: Llama3.2: ToolHop test-rand zero-shot 26.5, few-shot 29.9, RimRule 31.1; unseen 35.1 / 37.9 / 43.1. BFCL rand 50.1 / 54.5 / 56.6. MDL vs prompt consolidation: ToolHop 31.1 vs 27.5; BFCL 56.6 vs 52.1. Rules: 72 to 67 (ToolHop), 151 to 121 (BFCL). Small-data BFCL Multi-Turn (90 train, 4 rules): 55.2 to 62.1 rand, 46.0 to 60.0 unseen.
limits: Length weight alpha tuned on end-to-end accuracy. Gains are 2 to 8 points, one small model in the table I read; no token totals. Two-part code, not NML.
agent_relevance: First agent-level test that a two-part MDL objective beats a prompted summary. Supports a rule store pruned by length-versus-fit.

source: Nair and Wang (2024) MIDGARD: Self-Consistency Using Minimum Description Length
finding: MDL aggregates edges across 10 sampled reasoning graphs: keep properties that save bits, reject ones seen in few samples. Beats greedy decoding on argument-structure, explanation-graph and commonsense tasks.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, T=10 samples, 5 seeds. ExplaGraph: greedy StCA 23.7, SeCA 7.6, G-BS 18.6; MIDGARD 30.3 / 17.7 / 22.4. Code-Llama greedy 36.6 / 12.4 / 28.4 vs MIDGARD 39.4 / 20.2 / 29.7. Returns diminish with samples on ESSAYS; steady gains on ExplaGraph.
limits: Compared with greedy decoding and ablations, not a Bayes aggregator. Alpha needs tuning (alpha 0.5 drops all edges on Code-Llama). Metric direction of the GED column was unclear in extraction.
agent_relevance: MDL is a practical way to merge samples into one structure rather than pick one. Relates to merge operators in the scaffold.

source: Authors not read (2025) Predictable Compression Failures: Order Sensitivity and Information Budgeting (arXiv 2509.11208)
finding: Order sensitivity of evidence grows like log n, and a uniform mixture over permutations has a positive Jensen gain. This directly tests shuffle-averaging, but on 7-9B models, not frontier reasoning models.
numbers: 3,059 items, n from 3 to 60 chunks, 16 banded permutations each. Qwen2-7B: Jensen gap 0.1041 nats/token, slope b=0.377 (95% CI 0.319-0.435), R2 0.742. Llama-3.1-8B: gap 0.00982, b=0.147 (0.109-0.184), R2 0.515. Positive gap for 54 of 58 n values. Held-out audit of 528 items with fixed information gate: 0.0-0.7% hallucination, 20.6-27.9% abstention.
limits: Visible text reports log-loss gain, not an accuracy gain, from mixing. About 16 forward passes per item (97,888 in experiment 1). Bernoulli predicates only. No reasoning models in the part I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for frontier reasoning models. Shuffle-averaging lowers loss in small models but multiplies tokens by m, so it is not equal-token unless m is small.

source: Arora et al. (2024) Bayesian Scaling Laws for In-Context Learning (post-training and jailbreak sections)
finding: On GINC, SFT shifts the prior abruptly toward the favoured task, and the threshold grows with model size. On 7 instruct LLMs the Bayesian law is said to predict when suppressed behaviours return under many-shot prompting, but non-Bayesian laws fit about as well.
numbers: Models: Gemma 1.1 2B, Gemma 2B/7B, Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Llama 3.1 8B/405B. Real-world mean NRMSE: logistic 0.1599, Bayesian 0.1628, bounded 0.1637, power 0.1675; most differences not significant. Extrapolation fits the first 5% of the curve. Llama 3.1 8B base vs instruct: instruct lowers the prior on unsafe behaviours but the posterior still saturates.
limits: Same authors fit and test; no independent replication found. No numeric jailbreak rates in text (figures only). The GINC table read by my fetch disagreed with the cross-checker's corrected values, so use those (b15/c05 corrections) for GINC.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no independent fit found. Treat prior shift as a descriptive fit, not a validated mechanism.

source: Authors not read (2025) In-Context Learning Strategies Emerge Rationally (arXiv 2506.17859)
finding: A hierarchical Bayesian model with a memorising predictor and a generalising predictor explains transformer next-token predictions through training. Strategy choice trades loss against complexity, an MDL-style tradeoff.
numbers: Abstract only: predicts transformer predictions 'almost perfectly' across training; predicts that the switch time from generalising to memorising grows superlinearly with task diversity. No numbers read.
limits: Only the abstract was opened. Small transformers trained on task mixtures, not pretrained LLMs.
agent_relevance: Independent support for loss-plus-complexity (two-part code) as a model of ICL; relevant to gaps 6 and 10 but at toy scale.

source: Authors not read (2025) What Characterizes Effective Reasoning? Revisiting Length, Review, and Structure of CoT (arXiv 2509.19284)
finding: Across 10 reasoning models, shorter CoT correlates with higher accuracy within a question, and the fraction of failed steps predicts correctness best. Selecting by it beats random, and removing failed branches helps.
numbers: 10 models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking, Grok 3 mini, DeepSeek R1, R1-Distill-Qwen 32B/7B, Qwen3 235B/32B/8B, GPT-oss 120B/20B). HARP (50 x 6 levels), GPQA-D (198), AIME25 (30); 16 traces per question for correlations, 64 for top-1 selection. Failed-step-fraction selection roughly +5 to +13% over random on AIME25. Editing out failed branches: R1 first-failure 20.89 to 29.42; last-failure 9.72 to 23.75; GPT-oss-120B 28.05 to 36.41.
limits: Qwen results anomalous (suspected contamination). Coefficients only in figures. Failed-step labelling uses an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: length is a weak negative predictor; a structural dead-branch measure predicts better. The schema should drop failed branches rather than carry bits with no evidence.

source: Authors not read (2026) Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory (arXiv 2610.34073)
finding: Most agent memory systems fall below plain chunked RAG. Memory loses value through information loss at construction and poor accessibility, not because stored content is wrong.
numbers: LongMemEval-s (500 questions): RAG scores 72.2 / 81.4 / 90.0 over three backbones (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-5.6 Luna); every listed memory system is below. OpenViking has no memory unit for 38.0% of sampled facts; MemoryOS keeps 98.4%. PersonaMem-v2 4B: Memory-R2 38.2 and MemOS 37.2 vs RAG 36.2.
limits: Does not test prequential gain, relevance, recency or loss change as predictors. Static, English, subsets, no frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no study found that scores a note by later-token loss. Baseline lesson: keep a recoverable path to the source, since compression alone loses value.

source: Authors not read (2026) When Should Models Change Their Minds? Contextual Belief Management (BeliefTrack, arXiv 2605.30219)
finding: LLMs fail at keeping a belief when told to, updating when corrected and ignoring noise. Prompting is inconsistent; RL with a belief-state reward fixes it. No Bayesian baseline.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B vanilla failure rates 99/98/97; Qwen3.5-9B Rule Discovery 47.0/60.0/83.7 (stay / update / isolation). Belief-tracking prompt raised Qwen3.5-9B update failure 60.0 to 69.0. RL cuts failures by 70.9% on average; steering 46.1%. SFT dropped GSM8K 83.3 to about 70.
limits: Two synthetic tasks, 7-9B models. Trained, not scaffolded.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: prompting alone does not give clean belief tracking in small models; no test of an explicit posterior table at equal tokens.

source: Gap-search log (2026-11-10): paper search and arXiv search for NML, luckiness, minimax regret in LLM work
finding: No LLM or agent paper using NML, luckiness functions or minimax-regret code selection was found. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API returned 429, so this is weak negative evidence. Two-part MDL (RIMRULE, MIDGARD) and BMA (Large Language Bayes) were found instead.
numbers: Queries: normalized maximum likelihood LLM; minimax regret luckiness language model; NML stochastic complexity in-context; arXiv title/abstract search for 'minimum description length' LLM gave 7 hits (RIMRULE, MIDGARD, MADIL, HyperSU, skill learning, originality, task planning).
limits: Absence of hits is not proof; coverage is titles and abstracts only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. NML is the subfield's unique claim and still has no agent test.
